lesson.title: The Graph of a Line: Every Solution, All at Once
lesson.summary: The graph of a line is the complete picture of every ordered pair that satisfies a linear equation, and it always forms a straight path across the coordinate plane.
lesson.body:
A linear function like y = 3x - 2 has infinitely many valid input-output pairs, since any real number can be plugged in for x. Listing every single one is impossible, but plotting several of them reveals a pattern: they all fall along the same straight path. That path, containing every ordered pair that makes the equation true, is called the graph of a line. Instead of checking pairs one at a time algebraically, the graph lets you see all the solutions at once, spread across the coordinate plane in a single continuous sweep.

Building this graph starts exactly where plotting points left off. Using the same function from the previous chapter, y = 3x - 2, three ordered pairs were already calculated: (0, -2), (1, 1), and (2, 4). Plotting these three points using the horizontal-then-vertical method from the plotting points chapter places them at three distinct locations. Once plotted, it becomes visually clear that a single straight line passes through all three, since the output increased by the same constant amount, 3, for each unit increase in input, and a constant rate of change is exactly what keeps a set of points from curving.

This connects to an important geometric fact: two points are enough to completely determine a unique straight line. Once you know that a relationship is linear, you technically only need two ordered pairs to draw its entire graph, since a straight line cannot bend or change direction between them. A third point is useful mainly as a check, to confirm the first two points were plotted correctly and the line really is straight, rather than being strictly necessary to define the line itself. This is different from many curved relationships, which can require several more points before their shape becomes clear, making straight lines unusually easy to graph with confidence.

Here is a worked example demonstrating that check. Using the equation y = 3x - 2, predict a fourth point at x = 3 before plotting it: y = 3(3) - 2 = 9 - 2 = 7, giving the ordered pair (3, 7). If this point, when plotted, falls exactly on the straight line already drawn through (0, -2), (1, 1), and (2, 4), that confirms the graph was constructed correctly. Since the output kept climbing by exactly 3 for each step of 1 in the input, from 4 at x = 2 to 7 at x = 3, the new point does indeed continue the same straight path without any deviation.

The graph of a line is more than a picture; it is a tool for reading information directly off a drawing instead of recalculating it algebraically every time. Two particularly useful landmarks on any line's graph are the exact points where it crosses each axis, which are covered next as the x-intercept and y-intercept. Both of those landmark points are themselves ordered pairs, found on this same line, so all of the plotting skills from earlier chapters carry forward directly into locating them.
